title: Forgiveness in Islam and Christianity
subtitle: Can God forgive directly without making wrongdoing or its victims disappear?
summary: Islam holds that God can forgive a sincerely repentant person directly while preserving personal responsibility and the rights of those harmed. Christian accounts place forgiveness within Christ's saving work, but differ about why the cross was necessary. The Islamic argument must therefore address justice and revelation rather than caricature every Christian account as a demand for blood.

seo.metaTitle: Forgiveness in Islam and Christianity: Cross or Repentance?
seo.metaDescription: The Islamic case for direct forgiveness, the serious Christian argument for atonement, and why mercy must not erase victims' rights.

sections.title: Mercy Without Transferred Guilt
sections.body:
Islam's claim is that God can pardon the repentant person without transferring moral guilt to someone innocent. The offender must face the truth and change; those harmed do not lose their rights because the offender has prayed.

This account is worth considering because it keeps three things together: mercy is genuinely available, responsibility remains personal, and forgiveness is not permission to deny the harm.

sections.title: The Question Is What Makes Forgiveness Possible
sections.body:
Forgiveness does not mean calling betrayal good or pretending that no betrayal occurred. It concerns how a real wrong can cease to define a person's standing before God.

Islam answers through God's own mercy and sincere repentance. Historic Christianity grounds forgiveness in Christ's saving work, often discussed under the term atonement: reconciliation between God and sinners. The disagreement is not between a faith that values love and one that values law. It concerns what establishes the sinner's return to God and why.

sections.title: Does Justice Require Someone to Be Punished?
sections.body:
A punishment can recognize a wrong without repairing everything it damaged. Likewise, bearing another person's costs is not the same as becoming morally responsible for that person's choice. These distinctions make the question of atonement more demanding than a simple financial analogy.

Some Christians emphasize Christ bearing the penalty of sin; others emphasize reconciliation, healing, and victory over death. The latter themes appear prominently in the [Orthodox account of redemption](https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/doctrine-scripture/the-symbol-of-faith/redemption). Islam rejects making another person's saving suffering the condition of pardon. These different Christian accounts mean the disagreement cannot be reduced to a single debt-payment formula.

sections.title: Even Christian Thinkers Qualify Necessity
sections.body:
[Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae III, question 46, article 2](https://www.newadvent.org/summa/4046.htm), allows that God could have delivered humanity otherwise, while maintaining that the cross fulfills the divine plan. He also argues that forgiving an offense against oneself without satisfaction need not be unjust.

This does not make Aquinas a Muslim or remove the cross from his theology. It shows why the Islamic case should not depend on saying every Christian believes God is intrinsically unable to forgive. The issue includes God's chosen means, which is a question of revelation as well as reasoning.

sections.title: The Quran's Account of Direct Return
sections.body:
Quran 4:110 promises forgiveness and mercy to the person who wrongs himself and then seeks God's forgiveness. Quran 39:53 addresses even grave wrongdoing without making despair a virtue.

The return has substance. Quran 3:135 praises seeking forgiveness without knowingly persisting, and 20:82 joins repentance with faith and continued guidance. Quran 25:70 connects repentance with changed action; 2:222 speaks of God's love for those who repent. Quran 6:164 keeps moral burden personal throughout.

sections.title: Reading the Biblical Evidence in Context
sections.body:
Hebrews 9:22 connects forgiveness with blood in its discussion of purification and covenant, while 1 Peter 2:24 describes Christ bearing sins. These are serious grounds for the Christian account, not incidental phrases to dismiss.

The Bible also depicts mercy in response to return: Nineveh in Jonah 3:10, the contrite heart in Psalm 51:16–17, the tax collector in Luke 18:13–14, and the returning son in Luke 15:20–24. Matthew 6:14–15 and 1 John 1:9 connect forgiveness with forgiving others and confession.

Christians can read these scenes as benefits of Christ's work, including before the crucifixion. The scenes therefore do not create an automatic contradiction. They do show that repentance and divine mercy are deeply rooted in the biblical picture.

sections.title: The Strongest Reply: God Gives Himself
sections.body:
A Christian may object that the cross is not an innocent third party being forced to rescue sinners, but God's voluntary self-giving through the Son. That reply changes the argument. Merely describing the cross as a helpless victim's payment does not address historic Christian belief.

The Islamic response is that voluntary suffering, however loving, does not by itself establish that divine forgiveness requires it or that Jesus is God incarnate. Those are further claims needing evidence. Islam's alternative keeps the repentant person accountable and locates pardon in God's merciful judgment. [Incarnation Explained](/articles/incarnation-explained) addresses the identity claim behind the Christian reply.

sections.title: An Objection From the Person Who Was Harmed
sections.body:
Direct forgiveness can sound unfair if an offender prays and then demands that a victim act as though nothing happened. Islam does not give an offender that authority. [Dar al-Ifta's ruling on restitution](https://www.dar-alifta.org/en/fatwa/details/2901/donating-the-reward-of-fasting-to-a-person-i-owe-him-money), for example, rejects using devotional acts in place of returning money wrongfully taken.

Not every injury can be fully repaired in this life. The Islamic account therefore includes [final judgment](/articles/the-day-of-judgment), not a declaration by the offender that every claim has vanished. Mercy cannot be used as pressure on a harmed person to surrender safety or trust.

sections.title: Why Direct Forgiveness Remains Compelling
sections.body:
The moral strength of the Islamic account is not simply its lack of a ritual intermediary. It makes repentance answer to the wrong itself: deception must stop, another person's claim must be addressed, and the person seeks mercy rather than declaring innocence.

It also refuses the idea that perfect justice must exclude every act of pardon. A wise Judge can know the difference between genuine return and manipulation. The question of whether the Quran reliably reveals that Judge remains essential, and is examined in [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran).

sections.title: Forgiveness With a Practical Direction
sections.body:
[Sin and Repentance](/articles/sin-and-repentance) sets out what a sincere return looks like. Beginning with an actual obligation is more meaningful than treating forgiveness as a debate detached from conduct.

Islam's invitation is to the God who hears repentance directly: neither an excuse to trivialize evil nor a reason to believe that past evil makes return impossible.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Does every Christian teach that God cannot forgive without payment?
A: No. Aquinas allows another possible means of deliverance while affirming the cross as God's chosen plan. Orthodox and Protestant explanations also should not be reduced to one formula.

Q: Does Hebrews 9:22 settle every biblical case of forgiveness?
A: It must be read within its argument about purification and covenant. Leviticus 5:11 permits a poor person's flour sin offering; the narratives discussed above also depict forgiveness connected with return. Christians interpret these within Christ's work, so a bloodless scene alone does not refute their whole account.

Q: Does direct forgiveness cancel a victim's claim?
A: No. Sincere return does not make another person's rights disappear. Repayment or an appropriate release of the claim is not replaced by an unrelated devotional act.

Q: Does Islam understand Christ's death as atoning for other people's sins?
A: No. Islam honors Jesus as God's messenger and does not make his suffering the condition of pardon. Quran 6:164 keeps moral responsibility personal.

Q: What is the practical next step after wrongdoing?
A: Stop the wrong, regret it, resolve to change, seek God's forgiveness, and address rights that have been violated. Complicated cases require qualified guidance rather than a formula that causes further harm.

sections.title: Sources and Further Study
sections.body:
The scripture cards preserve the selected passages rather than substituting paraphrases for their approved wording. Aquinas and the Orthodox source illustrate why Christian theories of atonement must be distinguished.

The Christian works below develop different accounts of Christ's saving work. The Islamic work addresses repentance itself; these are different subjects that meet in the question of forgiveness.

quranVerses.arabic: ۞ قُلْ يَٰعِبَادِىَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا۟ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا۟ مِن رَّحْمَةِ ٱللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا ۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
quranVerses.translation: Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves [by sinning], do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَمَن يَعْمَلْ سُوٓءًا أَوْ يَظْلِمْ نَفْسَهُۥ ثُمَّ يَسْتَغْفِرِ ٱللَّهَ يَجِدِ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورًۭا رَّحِيمًۭا
quranVerses.translation: And whoever does a wrong or wrongs himself but then seeks forgiveness of Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِلَّا مَن تَابَ وَءَامَنَ وَعَمِلَ عَمَلًۭا صَٰلِحًۭا فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ يُبَدِّلُ ٱللَّهُ سَيِّـَٔاتِهِمْ حَسَنَٰتٍۢ ۗ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ غَفُورًۭا رَّحِيمًۭا
quranVerses.translation: Except for those who repent, believe and do righteous work. For them Allah will replace their evil deeds with good. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا فَعَلُوا۟ فَٰحِشَةً أَوْ ظَلَمُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَهُمْ ذَكَرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ فَٱسْتَغْفَرُوا۟ لِذُنُوبِهِمْ وَمَن يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ وَلَمْ يُصِرُّوا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلُوا۟ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ
quranVerses.translation: And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves [by transgression], remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins - and who can forgive sins except Allah? - and [who] do not persist in what they have done while they know.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَيَسْـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلْمَحِيضِ ۖ قُلْ هُوَ أَذًۭى فَٱعْتَزِلُوا۟ ٱلنِّسَآءَ فِى ٱلْمَحِيضِ ۖ وَلَا تَقْرَبُوهُنَّ حَتَّىٰ يَطْهُرْنَ ۖ فَإِذَا تَطَهَّرْنَ فَأْتُوهُنَّ مِنْ حَيْثُ أَمَرَكُمُ ٱللَّهُ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلتَّوَّٰبِينَ وَيُحِبُّ ٱلْمُتَطَهِّرِينَ
quranVerses.translation: And they ask you about menstruation. Say, "It is harm, so keep away from wives during menstruation. And do not approach them until they are pure. And when they have purified themselves, then come to them from where Allah has ordained for you. Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَإِنِّى لَغَفَّارٌۭ لِّمَن تَابَ وَءَامَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَٰلِحًۭا ثُمَّ ٱهْتَدَىٰ
quranVerses.translation: But indeed, I am the Perpetual Forgiver of whoever repents and believes and does righteousness and then continues in guidance.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: قُلْ أَغَيْرَ ٱللَّهِ أَبْغِى رَبًّۭا وَهُوَ رَبُّ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ ۚ وَلَا تَكْسِبُ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ إِلَّا عَلَيْهَا ۚ وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌۭ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ ۚ ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُم مَّرْجِعُكُمْ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ
quranVerses.translation: Say, "Is it other than Allah I should desire as a lord while He is the Lord of all things? And every soul earns not [blame] except against itself, and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you concerning that over which you used to differ."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way. God relented of the disaster which he said he would do to them, and he didn’t do it.

For you don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness; by whose stripes you were healed.

“He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ “But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe, and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let us eat, and celebrate; for this, my son, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ They began to celebrate.

“‘But if he can’t afford two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, then he shall bring his offering for that in which he has sinned, one tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it, and he shall not put any frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering.

furtherReading.title: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)
furtherReading.author: Anselm of Canterbury
furtherReading.note: A primary medieval Christian argument for satisfaction and Christ's saving work; not the only Christian account of atonement.

furtherReading.title: Christus Victor
furtherReading.author: Gustaf Aulén
furtherReading.note: A theological study of differing Christian accounts of redemption, including victory over evil.

furtherReading.title: The Cross of Christ
furtherReading.author: John Stott
furtherReading.note: An evangelical defense of penal substitution, included so that the position can be considered in a developed Christian form.

furtherReading.title: On Repentance (Kitab al-Tawba, from Ihya Ulum al-Din)
furtherReading.author: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali
furtherReading.note: An Islamic treatment of sincere repentance and moral renewal.
